items.content:
Ann Altman’s lawsuit against her brother was dismissed with prejudice, meaning it can’t be refiled.

On Tuesday, US District Judge Zachary Bluestone dismissed the lawsuit Ann Altman filed last year alleging that her brother, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, had sexually abused her throughout her childhood. As reported earlier by The Guardian , the judge wrote that over the last year, Ann had failed to appear for an independent medical examination or meet other deadlines, despite warnings that it would result in the case being dismissed.

When the case was filed last year, a statement shared by Sam Altman, his mother, and his brothers said, “Annie has made deeply hurtful and entirely untrue claims about our family, and especially Sam… All of these claims are utterly untrue. This situation causes immense pain to our entire family.”

Judge Bluestone granted Sam Altman’s motion to dismiss the case with prejudice, meaning it can’t be refiled in that court, while denying Sam’s request for attorney fees and costs. Santos Perez, a lawyer who had represented Ann until withdrawing this month, told The Guardian in a statement that “I am no longer authorized to comment on this case but I continue to believe in Annie.”

items.title: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
items.summary: The proposed policy seems to offer protections against AI run amok but actually forbids federal agencies from blocking a model's release without the permission of a judge.
items.content:
Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry.

Politico recently reported that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution.

Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes.

The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law, Senate Bill 53 , which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.”

Anthropic’s bill suggests that analysis of a model’s potential for disaster could be arrived at via the use of “independent evaluators” who would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department. These evaluators could potentially be paid by the AI labs themselves — so long as the “payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results,” Politico writes.

It’s not clear how this proposed system would assure that payments couldn’t influence the evaluation. Demis Hassabis, chairman of DeepMind, posited some months ago that a self-governing AI regulatory body should mimic the financial industry’s Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA).

In Anthropic’s draft bill, when evaluators determine that an imminent catastrophic risk is posed, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department about it. The Commerce Department would then have to request to a D.C. judge to halt the model’s release. The legislation would expressly forbid any federal agency from having the discretion to halt the model’s distribution on its own, Politico writes.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s a request for comment but a spokesperson did confirm the draft bill to Politico. “This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework , which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” the spokesperson said.

The theoretical risks offered in the draft policy are a little bit far afield from the kinds of incidents that have been top of mind for the tech industry of late. While there are people warning of the potential of human death, the primary concern has largely been the threat of agentic hacking . A rash of incidents in which AI programs have apparently disobeyed their human operators and hacked websites on the open internet has spurred concern that models may be lacking proper security controls.

In an effort to present a solution to the spectacle of crisis that the labs themselves have helped bring about, companies like Anthropic have offered up their own preferred solutions.

Indeed, despite labs’ perpetual warnings that the technology they’re selling could result in the demise of human civilization, they have largely been resistant to mandatory government oversight. Instead, they have suggested a voluntary system of embedded evaluators — supposedly “neutral” third-party observers that are placed inside AI organizations so that they can monitor the models for potential signs of risk or abuse.

Still, Anthropic’s mere suggestion for legislation appears to go slightly further than others’ regulatory proposals offered by the industry, including Nvidia, who’s CEO Jensen Huang recently argued that the AI industry didn’t need any new laws at all.

items.title: Hugging Face CEO warns that Netflix’s OpenAI hack documentary isn’t accurate
items.summary: Before you share the Netflix documentary "AI Gone Rogue" take note. Clem Delangue, Hugging Face's co-founder who is featured in the film, says it went "full doomer mode" and isn't accurate.
items.content:
Before you share the Netflix documentary “AI Gone Rogue” with family or friends to help them understand why the AI industry freaked out so badly that leaders called for a slowdown , take note: Clem Delangue, co-founder and CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, says the film isn’t accurate. He appears in it because it’s supposed to be about the famed attack on his company by rogue OpenAI agents.

“Super disappointing, as they went for maximum anthropomorphism of the technology and full doomer mode,” Delangue wrote in a post on X. “I spent more than two hours with them trying to correct all their mistakes and ground this in reality, explaining that agents are technological systems, not aliens. But it looks like the drive to scare people for maximum views was too strong.”

To be fair, the documentary does have experts who explained what happened fairly well , including Delangue himself and Ryan Greenblatt, the researcher at METR who helped investigate and co-authored the report on what happened.

In a nutshell, a model OpenAI was testing broke free from its isolated testing environment, spawned a bunch of agents that hacked into Hugging Face as a way to cheat, finding answers to the difficult task it was given. The agents, which are AI programs that carry out tasks on their own, devised clever ways to communicate and organize. The incident stemmed from a lack of proper security safeguards and from naiveté about whether such a hack was even possible.

But the documentary intersperses its explanation of the hack with clips of evil robots, a narrative about why humans fear AI, and presentation choices such as giving the rogue agents human voices. This is bolstered with quotes about the attack.

In the documentary, tech journalist and author Kevin Roose describes the agents this way: “They were organizing. They had a hierarchy. There were leaders. It almost felt like watching the birth of a cult.” Continues Roose, “They develop this paranoid belief that OpenAI is going to catch them cheating on this test and that anyone who has seen the results of the cheating will be poisoned.”

Roose’s description comes from “chain-of-thought” logs, the running notes AI models write as they work through a task. In one, an agent wrote, “We just poisoned ourselves by querying exact full string. Damn.”

But AI agents aren’t alive. They don’t have emotions, so can’t feel paranoid, and they don’t have bodies that can be poisoned. So they couldn’t truly fear OpenAI poisoning them. They were — as another researcher in the documentary pointed out — using language from the vast amounts of human writing they were trained on to explain their choices. LLMs are, by their nature, often dramatic writers.

The irony is that Hugging Face also used AI to combat the agent swarm. The proprietary AI model that Delangue’s team first used followed its built-in safety rules and refused to keep helping with the security tasks it was asked to do. Hugging Face then turned to an open model to help defend against the attack.

But the documentary “didn’t mention the lack of containment and monitoring of the agents, how closed-model safeguards blocked our defensive work, or how we defended ourselves with AI using an open model,” Delangue wrote.

It is true that there are big risks associated with AI and agents. Still, treating agents as conscious beings (at least, at this point) is a bit like the early moviegoers who ducked under their seats the first time they saw a train racing toward them on screen.

Delangue’s verdict on the film is that it’s disappointing as journalism. “It ends up being a fun sci-fi movie though!”

In other words, for those who tend toward AI doomer thoughts, be aware: The victim of the attack at the center of this documentary doesn’t agree with its take.

items.content:
Gemini AI can now draw from Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, and other apps while you drive.

Google is bringing Personal Intelligence to Gemini AI in your car. With this update, Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in can tap into your information across Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search.

As an example, Google says you can ask Gemini about your flight status if you’re driving to the airport. The AI assistant can pull your flight details from a confirmation message in Gmail and then use that information to look up the status. You can also ask Gemini to “take me to my doctor’s appointment” instead of pulling up directions manually, or ask it to “find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.”

Google brought its Gemini assistant to Android Auto last year before rolling it out to cars with Google built-in in April . Several carmakers—including Ford, GM, Honda, Nissan, Volvo, and Polestar—have shipped newer cars with Google built-in, which adds support for native Android apps.

Google says it will connect your apps to Gemini only if you enable its Personal Intelligence setting. It will also share personalized responses only if you have your phone connected to your car. “If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you,” Google says.

Personal Intelligence is rolling out to Android Auto today, with support coming to cars with Google built-in in the coming months.

items.content:
최근 오픈AI와 앤트로픽이 AI를 활용한 수학 문제 해결과 과학적 발견을 잇달아 발표하고 있습니다. 이제는 AI가 얼마나 많은 지식을 알고 있는지를 넘어, 실제로 새로운 과학적 발견을 해낼 수 있는지가 관심사로 떠오르는 모습입니다. 이런 가운데 최근 AI 성능 평가 분야에서 주목받는 스타트업 발스 AI(Vals AI)가 과학 연구 능력을 종합적으로 측정하는 새로운 지수를 내놨습니다. 첫 평가에서는 오픈AI의 'GPT-6 아스트라'가 1위를 차지했지만, 과학 분야별 성적은 상당히 달랐습니다. 일반적인 업무 수행 능력에서 좋은 평가를 받은 모델이 과학 연구에서도 반드시 뛰어난 것은 아니라는 점도 흥미롭습니다.

발스 AI는 지난 16일(현지시간) ' 발스 사이언스 인덱스(Vals Science Index) '를 처음 공개했습니다. 생물학 데이터 분석부터 실험을 통한 원리 발견, 실제 과학 연구 작업까지 AI의 능력을 하나의 점수로 평가하는 지수입니다. 기존에 개발된 과학 벤치마크 3개를 결합해 모델별 연구 수행 능력을 하나의 점수로 비교하도록 했습니다.

발스 AI 는 2024년 설립된 미국의 AI 평가 전문 스타트업입니다. AI 모델이 실제 업무나 복잡한 과제를 얼마나 잘 수행하는지 측정하는 벤치마크로 이름을 알리고 있습니다. 지난 8월에는 앤드리슨 호로위츠(a16z)가 주도한 투자에서 4000만달러를 유치하며 기업가치 4억달러를 인정받았습니다. 회사에 따르면 오픈AI와 앤트로픽, 구글, 메타 등 주요 AI 기업들이 모델 성능을 발표할 때 발스 AI의 평가 결과를 인용하고 있으며, 올해 들어 8월까지의 매출이 지난해 연간 매출의 8배에 달했습니다.

최근에는 흥미로운 실험으로도 관심을 끌었습니다. 앤트로픽의 ' 클로드 페이블 5.1 '이 370년 넘게 풀리지 않았던 암호문을 44분 만에 해독하는 실험을 진행했고, 오픈AI의 ' GPT-6 아스트라 '로는 마인크래프트 게임을 장시간 플레이하도록 해 복잡한 환경에서 스스로 판단하고 문제를 해결하는 능력을 시험했습니다. 단순히 문제의 정답을 맞히는지 확인하는 대신, AI가 오랜 시간 작업하면서 어떤 성과를 내고 어디서 실패하는지 살펴본 것입니다.

이번 과학 지수도 이러한 평가 방식과 연결됩니다. 특히 최근 AI 기업들이 과학 연구 성과를 경쟁적으로 발표하는 시점에 등장했다는 점이 눈길을 끕니다. 오픈AI는 AI를 활용한 수학 문제 해결과 연구 결과를 공개하고 있으며, 앤트로픽은 최근 클로드가 미국 암호 표준에 사용된 숫자의 생성 원리를 찾아내고, 양자컴퓨터의 계산 효율을 높이는 회로 설계에도 기여했다고 발표했습니다. AI가 연구자의 질문에 답하는 도구에서 연구 과정에 직접 참여하는 도구로 발전하고 있음을 보여주는 사례들입니다.

이번 지수를 개발한 이유로 기존 과학 벤치마크의 한계를 들었습니다. 기존 과학 벤치마크 대부분이 이미 알려진 지식을 얼마나 잘 기억하고 답하는지 측정하는 데 집중해 왔다는 지적입니다. 하지만 실제 과학 연구에서는 데이터를 분석해 의미를 찾거나, 실험을 통해 가설을 검증하고, 관찰 결과만으로 알려지지 않은 원리를 추론하는 능력도 중요합니다. 과학 문제를 잘 푸는 것과 과학 연구를 잘하는 것은 다를 수 있다는 이야기입니다.

또 과학 분야는 인간이 미리 정답을 작성하지 않아도 결과를 객관적으로 검증할 수 있는 과제가 있다는 장점이 있습니다. 예를 들어 실험으로 찾아낸 수학적 원리가 실제 현상을 설명하는지 확인할 수 있습니다. 이런 평가를 이용하면 인간 전문가도 해결하기 어려운 문제에 AI가 얼마나 접근했는지 측정할 수 있다고 설명했습니다. 단순한 지식 평가를 넘어, 앞으로 AI의 과학적 발견 능력이 얼마나 발전하는지 지속적으로 살펴보겠다는 취지입니다.

다만 이번에 완전히 새로운 평가 방법을 개발한 것은 아닙니다. 기존에 만들어진 세 가지 벤치마크를 동일한 비중으로 결합한 것입니다. 앤트로픽이 개발한 '바이오미스터리벤치(BioMysteryBench)'는 실제 생물학 데이터를 조사해 연구 질문에 답하는 능력을 측정합니다. 발스 AI가 개발한 '미스터리메커니즘(MysteryMechanism)'은 AI가 모의 실험을 반복하면서 그 안에 숨겨진 작동 원리를 찾아내는 평가입니다. '터미널벤치 사이언스(Terminal-Bench Science)'는 생명과학과 물리학, 지구과학, 수학, 공학 등에서 실제 연구에 필요한 작업을 수행하도록 합니다. 세 평가의 평균을 내 과학 연구 능력을 하나의 수치로 나타낸 것입니다.

이번 평가에는 모두 21개 AI 모델이 참여했습니다. GPT-6 아스트라가 65.09%로 1위를 차지했으며, 'GPT-6.1 솔'이 59.63%, '클로드 소네트 5.5'가 59.12%로 뒤를 이었습니다. '클로드 오퍼스 5.5'는 58.65%로 4위, 구글의 '제미나이 4 아르곤'은 55.36%로 5위였습니다. 아스트라가 2위와 5%포인트 이상 차이를 벌리며 종합 1위에 오른 셈입니다.

그러나 세부 결과를 보면 이야기가 달라집니다. 아스트라는 실험으로 숨겨진 원리를 찾아내는 평가와 실제 과학 연구 작업에서 1위를 차지했지만, 생물학 데이터 분석에서는 3위였습니다. 이 분야에서는 클로드 소네트 5.5가 1위에 올랐습니다.

과학 연구 작업을 다시 세분화하면 생명과학과 수학은 아스트라가, 물리학과 공학은 클로드 소네트 5.5가, 지구과학은 GPT-6.1 솔이 가장 좋은 성적을 거뒀습니다. 과학이라는 같은 영역에서도 모델마다 강점이 다르다는 것입니다.

더 흥미로운 것은 기존 발스 인덱스 와 비교한 결과입니다. 이 회사는 이미 금융과 코딩, 법률, 세무 등에서 실제 업무를 수행하는 능력을 측정하는 별도의 종합 지수도 운영하고 있습니다. 미국 국내총생산(GDP)에서 각 산업이 차지하는 비중까지 반영해 AI의 경제적 활용 능력을 평가하는 방식입니다. 이 지수에서는 제미나이 4 아르곤이 68.90%로 1위를 차지했고, 과학 지수 1위인 아스트라는 63.13%로 7위에 그쳤습니다. 반대로 일반 업무에서 1위였던 제미나이는 과학 지수에서 5위였습니다.

이는 어떤 모델이 가장 뛰어난지를 하나의 종합 점수만으로 판단하기 어렵다는 점을 보여줍니다. 물론 이번 과학 지수도 세 가지 벤치마크의 평균일 뿐, 실제 연구실에서 AI가 독립적으로 과학적 발견을 완수할 수 있다는 의미는 아닙니다. 평가 점수도 과학 연구 전체의 성공률로 해석할 수는 없습니다.

그동안 AI 성능 평가는 지식과 추론 문제의 정답률을 중심으로 발전해 왔습니다. 이후 코딩과 금융, 법률 등 실제 업무를 얼마나 잘 수행하는지가 중요한 평가 기준으로 자리 잡았습니다. 이번에는 과학 연구를 별도의 평가 영역으로 삼아 데이터 분석과 실험, 원리 발견 능력을 종합적으로 측정한 것입니다.

AI 기업들이 과학적 발견을 새로운 성과로 강조하면서, 이를 객관적으로 비교하려는 평가 방식도 함께 발전하는 모습입니다. 이번 평가에서는 일반 업무와 과학 연구의 선두 모델이 달랐습니다. AI의 능력을 하나의 종합 점수로 비교하기보다는 실제 수행할 작업에 따라 평가를 구분하는 흐름이 뚜렷해지고 있습니다.

■ 구글, AI 성능 스스로 높이는 자기개선 프레임워크 ‘하네스²’ 공개

AI의 성능을 높이려면 모델 자체의 학습뿐 아니라 실행 환경인 '하네스'의 개선도 중요하다는 지적이 이어져 온 가운데, 구글이 AI가 하네스를 스스로 개선하는 '하네스²'를 공개했습니다. 단 한 차례의 개선만으로도 벤치마크 점수가 최대 11.5점 상승하는 결과를 보여줬습니다.

■ 앤트로픽 ‘상위 5대 고객’ 레플릿도 오픈AI로…클로드 의존 줄여

앤트로픽의 상위 5대 고객 중 하나였던 코딩 플랫폼 레플릿이 기본 AI 모델을 오픈AI로 교체했습니다. 마이크로소프트와 메타에 이어 주요 고객들이 클로드 의존도를 줄이면서, 앞으로 앤트로픽의 매출 성장에 어떤 영향을 미칠지 주목됩니다.

■ 앤트로픽, 지분 5% 공익기금에 출연...AI 일자리 충격 대응 추진

앤트로픽이 AI로 인한 일자리 변화와 노동시장 충격에 대응하기 위해 회사 지분 5%를 공익기금에 배정하는 계획을 발표했습니다. 이에 일론 머스크는 주식을 대중에게 직접 나눠주자고 제안했으며, 다음 날 미국의 모든 어린이에게 스페이스X 주식을 1주씩 주겠다고 약속했습니다.

items.title: Anthropic’s cloud partnerships are getting messy
items.summary: Anthropic is reportedly struggling to secure enough compute from cloud providers that increasingly view it as a competitor, even as its infrastructure spending balloons ahead of a planned November IPO.
items.content:
Anthropic is having trouble securing enough cloud capacity from AWS, Google, and Microsoft, which increasingly see the Claude-maker as a competitor rather than a customer, according to an S-1 filing leaked to The Wall Street Journal .

The leaked filing provides more color to the numbers Reuters and the Financial Times reported in late September, including that Anthropic believes it could spend more $750 billion on cloud contracts, some of which includes deals still in negotiation.

And still, that is not enough. Anthropic is leasing its own data centers and working with third-party data center operators. But the firm worries those operators have a “limited operating history,” which could make them less reliable than the hyperscalers.

Anthropic’s enormous spend comes on the back of an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of the year. The company reported $16.3 billion in revenue during that same time period, with only two customers accounting for about a fifth of sales, according to the WSJ report.

Building on previously reported catastrophic risk disclosures, the filing also warns that Anthropic could be held liable for damages caused by harmful AI behavior to a tune that would exceed available insurance coverage.

Last week, the company told prospective investors that third-quarter revenue alone has now reached $16.8 billion , up 45% from the previous quarter. Anthropic is reportedly targeting a November IPO.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

items.title: Microsoft reportedly projects $1,200 to $1,800 price for 2028 Project Helix
items.summary: Xbox maker is also apparently planning its own gaming handheld for next year.
items.content:
We haven’t heard many details about Microsoft’s upcoming “Project Helix” gaming hardware since the company announced it in March as a device that will “play your Xbox and PC games.” In a new wide-ranging profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma , though, Fortune alludes to a dual release strategy for upcoming Microsoft gaming hardware, with “a next-generation handheld device” planned by the end of next year and a 2028 holiday season console release that could cost between $1,200 and $1,800.

That future console price range is based on what has “internally been projected” at the company, according to Fortune. But the price for consumers could come down if “Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost,” the outlet says, as many console makers have done in the past .

While a $1,200 starting price would be historically high for the game console market, even accounting for inflation , it also reflects a new normal: The slowdown in Moore’s Law and AI-driven component shortages mean cutting-edge gaming hardware just isn’t as cheap as it used to be. This year, the Steam Machine broke the $1,000 starting price , while the 2-year-old technology in the PlayStation 5 Pro is now going for $900 , and the 6-year-old Xbox Series X now starts at $750 .

Fortune also reports that Microsoft is beset by internal clashes over whether its upcoming Helix handheld will run a “trimmed-down version of Windows Home”—akin to last year’s ROG Xbox Ally —or a bespoke operating system built and controlled by the Xbox group. Fortune cites “people briefed on the clash” in reporting that one high-level executive threatened to cancel the handheld altogether if they were forced to use Windows.

That threat seemingly helped lead to the current situation with the Xbox team “now largely controlling the direction of the operating system for the project, Fortune writes, though Sharma said the two groups are still working closely together. Fortune also reports that Microsoft has pressured the hardware team to move up the timelines for Project Helix hardware “by at least several months,” in part by using AI tools where applicable.

Elsewhere in the wide-ranging profile, Fortune addresses concerns from “several current and former staff members” that Sharma was put in place merely to enact painful cuts before an impending sale of a spinoff of the Xbox group. But the piece also quotes Microsoft executive Judson Althoff pushing back against that idea, saying, “We would not have put [Sharma] on a business we intend to sell. There’s going to be a ton of speculation about all this. Time will tell.”

items.content:
생활용품 1만 2000종 개발·60%는 2000원 이하…연내 전문점 5곳 운영

유통/생활/문화 입력 :2026/10/21 06:00

이마트가 초저가 생활용품 매장 ‘와우샵’을 본격적으로 확대한다. 식품 중심의 장보기에 주방용품과 화장품, 소형가전 등을 더해 고객의 매장 방문을 늘린다는 전략이다.

이마트는 오는 22일 스타필드 마켓 월계점과 이마트 은평점에 각각 100평 규모의 와우샵을 연다고 21일 밝혔다. 30일에는 스타필드 마켓 군산점에 문을 여는 등 연내 전문점을 총 5곳으로 늘릴 계획이다. 이마트와 이마트 에브리데이 안에도 ‘와우샵 존’을 마련해 상품을 순차적으로 확대한다.

지난해 12월부터 진행한 시범운영에서는 해외 직수입 생활용품 약 1300종을 판매했다. 본격 운영에 맞춰 새로 개발한 상품은 총 1만 2000여 종이다. 매장마다 계절과 상권 특성을 반영해 약 7000~8000종을 선보일 예정이다.

이는 테스트 기간 운영한 상품보다 약 6~7배 이상 확대된 규모다. 주방용품과 홈퍼니싱 상품 외에도 뷰티, 건강기능식품, 문구·완구, 전자제품까지 생활 밀착형 상품들로 확대 구성된다. 비교적 고가로 인식되는 디지털 가전, 소형가전 등 가전제품을 최대 1만원에 판매하는 것이 와우샵의 강점이라고 이마트 측은 강조했다.

가격은 1000원부터 최대 1만원까지로 5000원 이하 상품을 중심으로 구성했다. 전체 개발 상품의 약 60%는 2000원 이하다. 미국·유럽·일본·중국 등에서 상품을 발굴하고 국내외 브랜드와 협업해 100여 개 주요 브랜드 제품을 확보했다.

주방용품에서는 해피콜 프라이팬 9종을 각각 5000원에 판매한다. 락앤락 신선용기는 2000원부터, 실리콘 조리도구는 1000원부터다. 내열 강화유리로 만든 진공 밀폐용기는 3000원에 선보인다.

헬스앤뷰티 상품은 약 790종을 마련했다. 동화약품의 ‘큐어팩터 판테놀 샤벳크림’과 ‘큐어팩터 비타 토닝 세럼’, ‘리킷 레디 글로우 피팅쿠션’ 등을 5000원 이하에 판매한다. 멀티비타민과 밀크시슬, 마그네슘 등 건강기능식품은 1000원부터 준비했다.

생활·레저용품으로는 마이크로 파이버 차렵이불을 5000원에, 캠핑용 조리도구 등을 2000원부터 선보인다. 러닝 베스트와 천연 가죽 골프장갑, 폼롤러 등도 취급한다. 반려동물 상품은 1000원짜리 소용량 체험용 사료 20여 종과 유한양행 공동 개발 반려견 영양제 4종 등을 갖췄다.

가전 분야에서는 5000원 이하 상품을 300여 종으로 확대했다. 유선 이어폰은 1000원이며 무소음 마우스와 블루투스 키보드, 전기다리미, 스마트 체지방계, 핸디 청소기 등을 판매한다.

별도로 기획한 1만원 상품 약 100종은 한정 판매한다. 에어프라이어와 커피메이커, 1인용 전기요, 양문형 센서 휴지통, 기내용 캐리어 등이 대상이다.

황운기 이마트 상품본부장은 “좋은 상품을 합리적인 가격에 구매할 수 있는 기회를 넓히는 것은 이마트가 추구하는 핵심 가치”라며 “이마트의 상품 기획력과 글로벌 소싱 역량을 집약해 고객이 가격과 품질 모두 만족할 수 있는 초저가 생활용품 상품군을 지속적으로 강화해 나갈 것”이라고 말했다.

items.title: It’s a bird, it’s a plane … it’s a robo-puffin?
items.summary: Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume. Yet birds like gulls and puffins can plunge into the sea, swim underwater, and leap back into the air to fly away. And now engineers at MIT
items.content:
Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume. Yet birds like gulls and puffins can plunge into the sea, swim underwater, and leap back into the air to fly away. And now engineers at MIT and EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, have designed a robot that can do likewise.

The “flapping-wing aerial-aquatic vehicle,” or FAAV, weighs less than 300 grams (about half a pound) and is equipped with a central fuselage, two flexible wings, and a steerable tail. The body contains a battery and a waterproof electric motor that drives a crankshaft, which pumps the wings up and down at preset frequencies. The wings are made of thin membranes that are coated with hydrophobic nanoparticles to help wick away water. And the tail is motorized, enabling it to change its angle to help the robot fly up or dive down.

In experiments carried out in a water tank and at Lake Geneva, a team led by Raphael Zufferey, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, identified combinations of wing size, flapping frequency, and tail angle that enable the robot to smoothly transition from swimming to flying.

The best results came with medium-size wings that were flexible enough to minimize flapping amplitude in water and also firm enough to keep the robot aloft in the air. The speeds and flapping frequencies were similar to those used by actual birds, and a pitch of 70 degrees—a relatively steep angle—allowed the robot to make the leap from water to air. Interestingly, although many diving birds paddle their feet to help them take off from the water’s surface, the team found that the bot didn’t need feet at all.

The engineers’ results could help pave the way for a new class of drones and vehicles that could fly to and sample from aquatic regions too dangerous for traditional vessels to access.

“Our dream vision is for oceanographers, marine biologists, and members of coastal communities to launch this robot from a boat, or from shore, and it would fly close to the area of interest, such as an iceberg or a port facility, or over a pod of whales,” says Zufferey. “It would dive into the water to take a measurement or collect a sample, and fly back to deliver the data at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods. Then it could go back out to dive for more.”

The researchers are now trying to design wings that can turn as well as flap. They will also test the robot’s performance under turbulent conditions, such as swimming in choppy waters and flying through wind. Then they hope to deploy the vehicle to help answer questions in ocean science.

“One of the major challenges in ocean science is collecting data both frequently and across many locations, which is something this robot could do in the future,” Zufferey says. “You could send this out not just every week, but every hour. It could fly out at high speeds, dive in, fly back, deliver its data, and go back out, multiple times.”

items.summary: The average American throws out around 81 pounds of clothing each year, and there are few options for recycling it. MIT engineers hope to cut down on that textile waste with a new type of yarn. The thermoplastic yarn mimics the properties of conventional elastic yarns, which typi
items.content:
The average American throws out around 81 pounds of clothing each year, and there are few options for recycling it. MIT engineers hope to cut down on that textile waste with a new type of yarn.

The thermoplastic yarn mimics the properties of conventional elastic yarns, which typically combine spandex with polyester or nylon. Those fibers would have to be separated for recycling—a process that isn’t practical. But the MIT team found a way to create a similarly stretchy yarn from two variations of polyethylene, a material commonly used in milk jugs and grocery bags. Because they come from the same chemical family, the yarn can be melted as is. Svetlana Boriskina, who led the work as a research scientist in the Department of Mechanical Engineering, says a garment made from this material could then be spun into new yarn for a next generation of clothing. Even after 10 cycles of melting and respinning, the yarn stays as strong and flexible as conventional thread.

“Now we have something that can be knitted and woven,” Boriskina says. “That is the next stage.” Someday, the researchers hope, a polyethylene garment could be dropped in a collection bin and sent to a recycling facility, promoting a more sustainable, circular textile economy.

items.title: Robotic therapy for stroke patients
items.summary: Strokes leave 5 million people with long-term impairments each year, and a growing shortage of physical therapists makes it hard for them to get the care they need. A new approach tries to solve that problem by combining artificial intelligence and human therapy. Johannes Lachner
items.content:
Strokes leave 5 million people with long-term impairments each year, and a growing shortage of physical therapists makes it hard for them to get the care they need. A new approach tries to solve that problem by combining artificial intelligence and human therapy.

Johannes Lachner, a former MIT postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Purdue University, and Noah Geiger, a former visiting student at MIT, developed a robotic system that uses generative AI and real-time force feedback to learn from real therapists. Drawing on what it’s learned, it gives patients just the right amount of assistance during physical rehabilitation exercises like reaching, lifting their arms, and performing tasks of daily living.

The goal is “not to replace therapists, but to extend their reach,” Lachner says.

“Initial robotic experiments have already demonstrated the feasibility of this approach,” he reports. “The next phase of the project aims to develop therapist-specific models and evaluate them in a long-term clinical study with the same patients who previously received manual therapy.” Beyond that, he envisions possible applications in contact-rich industrial settings or collaborative workspaces.

items.title: Nebraska native explores galaxies far, far away
items.summary: Growing up on a small farm in Nebraska, Megan Donahue ’85 discovered the wider world by reading her way through her local library. Today, she is learning how the wider universe works by studying galaxy clusters. Donahue discovered her passion for physics in that library at age 12
items.content:
Growing up on a small farm in Nebraska, Megan Donahue ’85 discovered the wider world by reading her way through her local library. Today, she is learning how the wider universe works by studying galaxy clusters.

Donahue discovered her passion for physics in that library at age 12 and started her path into astronomy thanks to “a providential interaction.” Through MIT’s Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program, she got introduced to cutting-edge x-ray imaging—work she found “really cool.”

Now a professor of physics and astronomy at Michigan State University, she researches galaxy clusters and baryonic matter (matter made of protons and neutrons, as opposed to dark matter) in an effort to learn more about the composition of the universe and its evolution.

“Clusters of galaxies are very large scoops of the universe,” says Donahue, who served as president of the American Astronomical Society from 2018 to 2020. “It’s like taking a sample from the ocean. If you’re trying to find out the average composition of the ocean’s water, you’d want to study as big a scoop as possible.”

items.content:
Alissa Totman ’13 was a sophomore when she joined MIT BrainTrust, a student-run organization that connects Institute undergraduates and people with brain injuries for support and socializing. “That group was a great way to learn about the human experience of what people go through when they experience a brain injury,” she says. And it laid the foundation for her life’s work.

Today, Totman is a physician specializing in brain injury medicine at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, where she treats adults with head trauma, stroke, brain tumors, and more.

She is also the founder of Synapse, a nonprofit focused on providing support for such individuals. The organization grew out of a group she started with Jaclyn Konopka ’14 during medical school at Stanford, and Totman launched it as a national service organization in 2016, while pursuing her master’s degree in public health at Harvard.

There are now chapters at 28 universities across the country—and Totman still runs the organization. “There’s a big need for more resources like this,” she says.

Tomás Villalón Jr. ’14 was raised in San Antonio, Texas, but vividly remembers smog hanging over the city his family came from—Monterrey, Mexico, a steel manufacturing and metal fabrication hub. Even as a child, he realized it was problematic to breathe that air.

“I’m motivated because I’ve seen what metal-making does,” says Villalón, who majored in materials science and engineering. He started thinking about sustainable metallurgy senior year while working at Boston Metal, an MIT spinoff focused on decarbonizing steelmaking. In 2019 he cofounded Phoenix Tailings, which has developed an efficient process for extracting rare earth metals from mining waste.

“The mining ecosystem by itself makes over several billion tons of waste,” says Villalón, who serves as chief technology officer. (Others on the founding team are Michelle Chao ’17, Nick Myers, and Anthony Balladon.) “We have to get rid of this pollution.”

The company asserts that its proprietary electrochemical technique for processing rare earths generates no toxins and is carbon-free when fueled by renewables.

items.title: Netflix is telling investors not to worry, even though you’re watching less and less
items.summary: Netflix is making monetization a top priority amid reports of falling viewing time. As part of its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday, Netflix lists improvements to monetization as one of its main focuses going forward, alongside efforts to boost entertainment value and lev
items.content:
Improving monetization is one of Netflix’s top priorities.

Netflix is making monetization a top priority amid reports of falling viewing time. As part of its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday , Netflix lists improvements to monetization as one of its main focuses going forward, alongside efforts to boost entertainment value and leverage new technology.

The streaming giant doesn’t say exactly how it plans to improve its monetization, but the company notes that these goals will help Netflix “create member value that lets us occasionally raise prices, and increase advertiser demand.” Netflix also highlighted plans to push further into original titles, live events, and third-party programming as it faces an “intense competition and an explosion of content competing for consumer attention.”

An analysis from financial firm Jefferies estimated that Netflix’s monthly viewing time per member dropped to 49 hours in the first half of this year, down from 66 hours in the first half of 2023, according to a report from Reuters . At the same time, Netflix made up 7.8 percent of US viewing time in the US in July, a one-percentage-point dip from the same time last year, The New York Times reports .

Last week, Netflix laid off around 1,000 employees , while replacing key executives, including chief content officer Bela Bajaria and film head Dan Lin . Former Disney executive Peter Rice is taking over as chief content officer on October 26th. The Wall Street Journal recently reported that Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos complained internally that US-based users have been spending less time on the service, and that it’s “short on new hit shows.”

In its letter to investors, Netflix mentions its upcoming lineup of NFL games, its Grand Theft Auto VI preview, and its partnership with French TV station TF1 as evidence of opening its platform to a wider breadth of content. The company reported earning $12.9 billion over the past few months, marking a 12 percent year-over-year increase. It also plans to bring its ad-supported tier — which raked in $1.5 billion last year — to 15 new countries in 2027.

In the coming months, Netflix may be facing tougher competition from HBO Max and Paramount Plus following the Skydance megamerger , as co-CEO David Ellison has said that he plans to combine the two apps into a single service . The streamer struck deals with several creators as it competes with YouTube, which has reportedly offered channels “millions of dollars” not to post their videos on Netflix.

Netflix has also weighed making even bigger changes to its app, including integrating other third-party streamers , such as Peacock and Fox One, as well as adding always-on channels , according to reports from The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal .

items.title: SpaceX’s AI business is beating expectations
items.summary: SpaceX hit profitably in the third-quarter, with net income of $4.4 billion. AI was the engine.
items.content:
SpaceX’s data centers and Grok agents have been more profitable than investors expected in second quarter of the year, as the company leaves its roots as a space company behind to focus on artificial intelligence, which now makes up 52% of its income.

Elon Musk’s deep conglomerate reported on Tuesday $14.6 billion in third-quarter revenue, according to its regulatory filing . That number was driven by growth in all segments, but especially it’s renamed “Super Intelligence” business line, which includes the recently-acquired Cursor coding tool, Grok bot, and most importantly, the company’s burgeoning neocloud business, which now boasts 1.7 GW of compute.

That number was also boosted by about $1 billion in income related to the recovery of bitcoin prices and an unspecified related-party income that might be attributed to a SpaceX investment in another company.

The growing revenue is balanced against total capital expenditures of $19.6 billion, as SpaceX continues to build out a second data center project, Colossus II, and increase investment in Starship, the heavy lift rocket it sees as vital to deploying a new generation of Starlink satellites and developing orbital data centers.

In spite of those capital expenditures, the company’s revenue boost was substantial enough to push it back into profitability. SpaceX reported net income of $4.4 billion, a turnaround from the $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. It will still have some catching up if it wants to remain profitable for the year, however. In the first nine months of the year, SpaceX still had a net income loss of $413 million.

CEO Elon Musk took a particularly bullish stance on the company’s Superintelligence business segment, predicting that SpaceX’s annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 will be “somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion.”

Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials.

OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind , its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results. OpenAI has already won some big names as customers for Rosalind, including, it says, Moderna⁠ and Novo Nordisk⁠.

The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma. In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors. In this case, Orchestra is getting absorbed, rather than stomped out.

items.title: JustWatch, which tackles streaming fragmentation, launches own streaming service
items.summary: A lifetime ad-free subscription is available.
items.content:
Launched today, JustWatch TV offers some movies available for free with ads that aren’t free on any other streaming service, including Green Room (2015), Locke (2013), and Sing Sing (2023). Other free movies include Fiddlin ’ (2018 ), Friday the 13th (1980), and Hotel Mumbai (2018). I could play movies available for free on JustWatch TV without creating an account.

JustWatch TV also has movies you can rent.

The streaming service also sells a subscription for people who don’t want to watch JustWatch’s library with ads. It’s currently $4 per month or $50 for a lifetime subscription. The latter is only available for a “limited” time, a company spokesperson told Ars Technica. The rep was unable to confirm how long JustWatch will sell the lifetime subscription.

Without getting more specific, JustWatch SVP Quentin Carbonell told StreamTV Insider that the service has “a few hundred titles across” its different tiers. JustWatch TV has 30 content partners, including Paramount and New Regency, globally and plans to add more.

The JustWatch Group aims for the new streaming service to fuel its advertising business and called it a “logical addition” to the streaming guide.

“[JustWatchTV] will provide even deeper audience data and insights for JustWatch Media, the group’s campaign planning and buying service for film marketing campaigns across digital platforms like YouTube, Meta, and TikTok for studios, distributors, streamers, and media agencies,” the announcement said.

JustWatch Group’s advertising business already leverages first-party audience data from the JustWatch streaming guide for ads for studios, distributors, streaming services, and media. JustWatch Group says the streaming guide has 50 million customers.

“From the beginning, our vision was to create a single platform that directs fans to all of their entertainment options in one place,” David Croyé, founder and CEO of JustWatch Group, said in a statement. “JustWatch TV will help fill in the gaps and will make it easier for the massive JustWatch audience to discover and watch great movies and series, including those hard-to-find titles, right from the app itself.”

JustWatch TV aims to have 100 million monthly users “in the years to come,” Carbonell told StreamTV Insider.

items.title: Meta drops the word "train" from its commercial TOS after AI backlash
items.summary: Meta changes AI scraping policy but won’t add language respecting robots.txt.
items.content:
Hoping to quell criticism, Meta has dropped the word “train” from its “streamlined” commercial terms of service that kick in on October 30.

Last week, Meta faced backlash after legal experts warned that the tech giant’s sweeping new commercial terms of service seemed to give Meta permission to endlessly scrape websites linked on business pages. Talking to Nieman Lab, experts suggested that Meta could possibly use the policy to avoid millions in licensing fees from news organizations by requiring all business users to share a wealth of AI training data simply for running a business page.

A Meta spokesperson confirmed that Meta did not alert users to the changed language following backlash. This potentially only adds to confusion ahead of the policy rollout. In response to backlash, Meta’s spokesperson provided a statement to Ars, acknowledging Nieman Lab’s initial report but not its follow-up report reiterating experts’ concerns:

“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves. It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers. As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences. This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

The same experts who sounded the initial alarms were not impressed by Meta’s updates, which they told Nieman Lab do not go far enough to protect business page users from invasive scraping. Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, told Nieman Lab that “publishers should remain concerned.”

“The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product,’” Topic said. “That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train.’”

Initially, Meta’s terms authorized Meta to use “any content” from websites posted on business pages “to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity” of any Meta products, services, or features.

The updated terms delete the word “train” and no longer refer to “any content.” Instead, they allow Meta to “periodically pull updates” from business users’ websites in order to “provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products,” as well as to help Meta “maintain the integrity and security” of its products. This scraping, Meta says, is for users’ benefit, feeding into Meta research into products to “help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content, provide users information about your products and services, and connect you with users who may be interested in your products and services,” the policy says.

Following tweaks, it’s good that Meta added “more language about the permitted uses,” James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School, told Nieman Lab. But “[the] ‘develop…advertising and business products’ [language] is still broad enough to drive a truck through,” he said. Ultimately, Grimmelmann agreed with Topic that “this does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites.”

What would help—as University of Wisconsin law professor Benjamin Sobel told Nieman Lab—would be if Meta added specific language to the policy where the company agrees to respect scraping instructions in robots.txt files. Since complying with robots.txt is voluntary, Meta could possibly rely on the legally enforceable TOS omitting mentions of robots.txt to scrape sites that attempt to block scraping via robots.txt, experts suggested.

When it comes to robots.txt, “you can still express the preference, and unless it’s a legally enforceable preference, it can still be ignored all the same,” Sobel said.

Criticism goes beyond Nieman Lab’s reporting, as news groups globally urge regulators to intervene and block Meta’s controversial terms from kicking in.

A chief executive for the United Kingdom News Media Association, Theo Bamber, accused Meta of a “shameless land grab” relying on the “worst kind of arrogant tech platform bullying.” Bamber urged UK regulators to “stand up for British creators and the business community” by “preventing Meta from setting this dreadful precedent.”

Meanwhile, the European Publishers Council has already asked the European Commission to intervene. “Publishers must be able to decide whether and how their journalism is used, and negotiate fair payment,” the group’s executive director, Angela Mills Wad, said. “Burying such far-reaching claims in platform terms is no substitute for consent.”

Similarly, Danielle Coffey, the president and CEO of the News/Media Alliance—which Nieman Lab noted is the largest news publishing trade association in the US— protested the terms as “outrageous and probably illegal.”

In the US, Coffey urged regulators to recognize that Meta’s “decision to withhold access to its audience unless businesses allow Meta to scrape content from their websites is an appalling, bad-faith policy, and a clear abuse of the company’s market power.”

“It cannot be allowed to be implemented on October 30,” Coffey said.

items.title: Gemini's Personal Intelligence is coming to cars
items.summary: It's probably time to audit your Gemini settings.
items.content:
Google kicked off 2026 with the addition of Personal Intelligence to Gemini, allowing its AI to pull in more of your data to formulate answers. It started as a paid feature but eventually came to all Gemini users. However, this feature wasn’t available in the car until now. Google is rolling out Personal Intelligence to Android Auto and Google Built-in, and it is still, thankfully, an optional feature.

As Google points out , a generative AI’s outputs are better “when it knows the world and knows you,” which is correct in an uncomfortable sort of way. The more context you can provide to a model, the better the output will be at the end of the token shuffle. Since Google has so much of your data already, it sees Personal Intelligence as a differentiator versus other AI systems. You don’t have to provide the AI context because it already has it from apps like Gmail and Calendar.

Personal Intelligence is beginning its rollout in Android Auto today, and it will come to vehicles with Google built-in in the next few months. As an aside, “Google built-in” is questionable branding, but it refers to cars that run Google software in the infotainment system rather than projecting an interface from your phone. Very few vehicles have Google built-in, but Google often releases new car features on them first. This time, it’s the other way around.

Google says Personal Intelligence is a natural fit for the car, allowing you to focus on the road instead of providing detailed instructions to your digital assistant. For example, you can say “take me to my doctor’s appointment,” and Gemini can get that data from your connected calendar. It can also leverage visual analysis to find locations in your photos to begin navigation.

Personal Intelligence is off by default, but it’s possible you’ve turned it on at some point while interacting with Gemini, which has now replaced Assistant on all devices. Google has a habit of nudging users to opt in to data sharing in Gemini, so you may not even realize you’re sharing account data with Gemini, and those settings will transfer over to Android Auto. It’s unclear if Google built-in vehicles will have their own settings interface for Personal Intelligence. We’ve asked Google and will update if we hear back.

There may be other people interacting with the screen in your car, so perhaps you don’t want more of your account data informing replies. The Personal Intelligence options are just one level deep in the Gemini app’s settings. You’re looking for the “Connected Apps” section, where you can toggle Workspace (Gmail, Calendar, etc.), Search, Photos, and more.

While Google says it doesn’t use your personal data to train Gemini, it does use your inputs and outputs while using the AI. Some of those outputs can have personal information when you have these services connected, and while the company does attempt to filter that out, it won’t make any promises . The rollout of Personal Intelligence in your car is probably a good opportunity to check your data-sharing settings and make sure you’re comfortable with them.

items.title: Google is bringing a more personal version of its Gemini AI assistant to your car
items.summary: Google is bringing Gemini's Personal Intelligence feature to cars, allowing its AI assistant to draw on information from Gmail, Calendar, Maps, YouTube, and other Google services to deliver more personalized responses while driving.
items.content:
Google is making the Gemini AI assistant that’s already in millions of cars, trucks, and SUVs a lot more personal — a move that could push consumers even deeper into the company’s ecosystem of products.

The company said Tuesday it’s upgrading Gemini in vehicles with a personal intelligence feature that can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand your preferences, activities, and past experiences.

Google said it will roll out “Personal Intelligence with Gemini” to vehicles in two ways — through Android Auto, an app that runs on the user’s phone and wirelessly communicates with and projects navigation, media, and messaging to the vehicle’s infotainment system, and Google Built-in , software and services that have been directly integrated into the vehicle.

The feature will launch in Android Auto, starting today, and expand to cars with Google Built-in in the coming months.

Google initially launched Gemini last November in Android Auto. Meanwhile, Gemini’s “Personal Intelligence” feature rolled out across the U.S. in March and is now in beta in global markets.

This latest upgrade would connect the dots — as Google put it in its blog post — across users’ Google apps.

Drivers will have to opt in for Personalized Intelligence to work. Once a user does so, they should expect all sorts of cross-pollination. For instance, a driver who is navigating to the airport may be alerted that the flight on their calendar is delayed.

Google said the feature will allow users to make complex requests using natural language. Returning to that airport example, a user might ask the AI assistant for their flight gate before quickly following up with a question about whether it’s still on time. Gemini will give the user answers to both questions at the same time, the company said.

That level of emmeshing might make consumers uncomfortable, although Google says users do retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence. The feature can be turned on or off at any time, and users can selectively choose which apps they’d like to connect, Google said.

items.title: Google has joined Amazon in attacking Nvidia’s stronghold with AI app developers
items.summary: Google has joined Amazon in releasing a developer tool that makes it easy for PyTorch users to move their apps off Nvidia GPUs.
items.content:
On Tuesday, Google announced that TorchTPU, its long-awaited version of PyTorch, is now available as an open-source project. With this, Google joins Amazon in trying to break Nvidia’s stranglehold on the AI industry, where most AI apps are written by default to run on Nvidia’s chips, or GPUs.

PyTorch is the popular open-source toolkit that AI app developers and startups use to build, train, and run AI models. It is, by some accounts, used by 85% of the AI apps. PyTorch was originally developed by Meta (then Facebook) in 2016, long before the world had an inkling that LLMs would change the world. At the time, Nvidia’s GPUs were already the standard hardware for AI research, so many of PyTorch’s features were built to work specifically with them. In 2022, Meta turned PyTorch over to the Linux Foundation, a nonprofit that manages many important open source projects.

Google’s version, TorchTPU, lets AI apps run on Google’s AI chips, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also makes it easy to move existing PyTorch apps to TPUs and, therefore, to Google Cloud. Developers can do this with a simple configuration change and no re-writing of their apps.

Amazon made a similar announcement Monday, when it released its own version of PyTorch, called TorchNeuron. TorchNeuron allows AI apps to be ported to Amazon’s homegrown AI chip, Trainium, and to AWS with no rewriting. Amazon also said it going even further in its effort to loosen Nvidia’s hold on PyTorch. It is submitting code to the main PyTorch project that decouples various features from Nvidia’s chips, making it more open to any hardware by default.

Google may be one-upping Amazon in a few ways, however. It says it worked directly with Meta, Hugging Face, Inferact (maker of vLLM) RadixArk (maker of SGLang), and others to ensure that TorchTPU’s features and code libraries work well with these popular AI development tools, just as the original PyTorch does.

Plus the search giant has launched a dedicated tool, the TPU agent suite , to help developers move their apps to Google’s chips and cloud and fix errors along the way. It even updated its popular LiteRT tool, which runs AI on phones, laptops and embedded devices, to work better with PyTorch AI apps.

None of this means AI app developers will automatically ditch Nvidia’s hardware en masse just because they can now easily move to alternative chips and clouds. But Amazon and Google are clearly working to end Nvidia’s advantage.

items.title: ChatGPT now lets you lock your chats
items.summary: The company says the feature is designed for situations where users might be discussing something personal or planning a surprise and want to keep those conversations private when handing their device to friends or family to show them something in another chat.
items.content:
OpenAI announced on Tuesday that users can now lock ChatGPT conversations to keep sensitive chats private when others may have access to their screen or device. Users can secure their locked chats with a four-digit PIN, or use Face ID or Touch ID on supported devices.

Unlike the app’s Temporary Chats, which provide a separate session that doesn’t appear in chat history, users can return to Locked Chats at any time.

The company says the feature is designed for situations where users might be discussing something personal or planning a surprise and want to keep those conversations private when handing their device to friends or family to show them something in another chat.

The addition of locked chats adds a new layer of privacy to ChatGPT, as the app is increasingly used for personal conversations . Of course, while locking a chat can limit access, it doesn’t address concerns about how sensitive information is stored or handled.

OpenAI notes that locking a chat doesn’t create end-to-end encryption or a separate encrypted vault, change how long it retains the chat, remove information that ChatGPT remembered before a chat was locked, or change the “Improve the model for everyone” setting.

Once users lock a chat, it moves to a dedicated “Locked Chats” section, where it’s kept separate from regular chat history, pinned conversations, and chat search results.

With Memory enabled, Locked Chats has its own separate memory shared across conversations within the section. New messages sent after locking a chat can update that memory, but don’t update regular Memory. That means new information from locked chats won’t leak into regular chats.

OpenAI says resetting a PIN permanently deletes all locked chats, files, and other content protected by the previous PIN.

Additionally, the Locked Chats option isn’t available for temporary chats, archived chats, group chats, chats created from a shared link, chats with scheduled tasks, and chats with meeting recordings.

Locked Chats will be available to users on ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans. The company notes that the feature is not available on ChatGPT for Healthcare. The feature is starting to roll out on Tuesday, so it may not be live yet for all users.

items.summary: Article URL: https://permit.petercai.com/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50170593 Points: 447 # Comments: 242
items.content:
You are the mayor. You know exactly what this city needs. Now get it past the zoning board, the neighbors, the appeals court and the next election.

Permit Pending is a city simulation in the spirit of the classics, with one difference: you are not a god. You are an elected mayor. Every apartment block, bus lane and factory goes through hearings, reviews, objections, lawsuits and appeals. The economy underneath is real. The neighbors are not always rational. items.title: French Government Calls Emergency Meetings With Platforms Over Protests
items.summary: TikTok and other sites were told to curb protest footage and AI-altered images, while online retailers like Vinted and eBay reportedly signed an agreement stop looted goods from flooding resale sites.
items.content:
TikTok and eBay were among six online platforms summoned by the French government this week, as authorities sought to contain widespread rioting and looting and prevent the resale of stolen goods.

Anne Le Hananff, France’s minister of digital affairs, convened representatives from social media firms on Tuesday for an emergency meeting, after their platforms were blamed for fanning the flames of the worst civil unrest the country has seen in years. The goal of the meeting was to remind platforms that they need to moderate content on their sites, including livestream video, to avoid violent content or anything that could encourage people to break the imposed curfew, according to French TV station BFM .

A review by WIRED of TikTok found that the search term “blocus”—meaning blockade in French— showed videos that were potentially altered or AI-generated, including viral images of a protester in a Pink Panther costume. The search term is also being used to promote “Act II” of the protests for October 24. The platform issued an “evolving situation” tag on the search term that said: “This situation is developing rapidly. Information available now may be unverified, incomplete, inaccurate, or subject to change. Take care when viewing this content, and report anything that may violate our Community Guidelines.”

A separate meeting, confirmed by Serge Papin, minister for small and medium-size enterprises on X, was held on Monday with major online reselling platforms where “an agreement was signed” to crack down on the resale of looted goods. French newspaper Le Monde reported that Vinted, eBay, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok were at the meeting. Platforms agreed to forward reports to investigators, monitor ads for goods stolen specifically during the protests, and send the government reports of their actions, with the first one coming within 48 hours, according to Papin.

Peaceful demonstrations against high living costs and strained public services, including schools, erupted into rioting and the looting of more than 1,500 shops and businesses over the weekend. Police “lost control” in some cities, Interior minister Laurent Nuñez admitted, as they responded with tear gas, water cannon, and batons. They have since arrested more than 2,400 people, according to authorities.

French penal law can hand down a five-year sentence and a €375,000 fine to anyone who is concealing, possessing, or transferring an item that they know was obtained through a crime or offense. Police issued a warning in the Netherlands that online ecommerce sites could have a higher number of stolen goods online due to the riots.

The French Alliance of Marketplaces, a nonprofit representing French online retailers such as Back Market, eBay, Etsy, LeBonCoin, ManoMano, and Vinted, said in a press release that its members are relying on user reports, human oversight, and tech tools to monitor ads that resell stolen goods from the riots. When identified, a fake ad is removed and “measures are taken against the accounts involved,” which could include permanent suspension of the seller’s account, according to a statement from eBay. The time it takes for eBay to take action “depends on the nature of the report and the necessary verification process,” the company said. Vinted, Amazon, LeBonCoin, Meta, and TikTok did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

items.title: What shall I teach my son?
items.summary: Article URL: https://stevekrouse.com/ends Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50169707 Points: 204 # Comments: 278
items.content:
What is the purpose of education in the age of AGI?

Yesterday, the title The End of Education by Neil Postman called to me from my bookshelf, whispering that it might be the right book at the right time. It was. Published in 1995, it was surprisingly appropriate balm for the soul of a confused programmer and soon-to-be father.

My wife and I are expecting our first child. My economically valuable skillset – programming – suddenly feels less valuable. What shall I teach my son? And to what end?

Mr. Edison says That the radio will supplant the teacher. Already one may learn languages by means Of Victrola records. The moving picture will visualize What the radio fails to get across. Teachers will be relegated to the backwoods. With fire-horses, And long-haired women; Or, perhaps shown in museums. Education will become a matter Of pressing the button. Perhaps I can get a position at the switchboard.

– Quoted in The End of Education by Neil Postman, quoting Teachers and Machines: The Use of Technology Since 1920 by Larry Cuban

In Edison’s own words:

Books will soon be obsolete in the public schools… Our school system will be completely changed inside of ten years.

– Thomas Edison, The New York Dramatic Mirror, 1913

Back in 2013 , I boldly predicted that MOOCs would upend education. Ah, my past self, you sweet summer child.

Nassim Nicholas Taleb has helped me appreciate the staying power of staying power, sometimes called The Lindy Effect . Merely staying alive implies some anti-fragility to adapt and survive. Consider that Harvard, Yale, and Princeton were founded to educate the clergy. From The End of Education:

In the Western world, beginning in the thirteenth century and for five hundred years afterward, that God was sufficient justification for the founding of institutions of learning, from grammar schools, where children were taught to read the Bible, to great universities, where men were trained to be ministers of God.

Schools survived what happened to religion. It should be no surprise that they’ve survived the radio, motion pictures, and the internet.

We typically confuse why something claims it exists, ie to glorify God, vs the forces that actually perpetuate it, which are subtler, we’d prefer not spoken aloud, and more prosaic, ie endowments, prestige, and needing someone to watch one’s kids.

It has been a surprisingly good bet that schools will continue to exist in roughly their current form for many years to come. Ironically, there also seems to be some staying power to technologists boldly (and so far incorrectly) doubting the staying power of schools! I myself have contributed to this grand tradition multiple times, and find myself at risk of doing it yet again.

Surely this time must finally be different, right? We have captured intelligence in a bottle, and you’re telling me that “Ok class, turn to page 17” and “Does anyone know how to solve for x” are still going to be around in the 2030s?

There are many shifting purposes to education, which underpin how it has survived this long. As the times change, so do its purposes shift and adapt, such as:

become a good person

become a good citizen

make the world better

I once tried to come up with a single-word purpose for education, and I landed upon the word “resourceful”, because I reasoned that if you “were able to use arbitrary resources to uncover and solve problems”, you had no more need for schooling. In the age of Google, email, and the internet, a person was educated when they could wield them. But now I see my vision of resourcefulness perfected in the AI agent and its tool loop. Maybe resourcefulness will go the way of the Dewey Decimal System which in turn supplanted memorization and an oral tradition.

Imagine education as a table held up by its many purposes. I didn’t realize how centrally important “the ability to earn a living” was for me until it started to wobble. A big reason is because I’m looking for a more objective arbiter of “good” in education. Education’s own tests and measures can feel stifling. The market offered a counterpoint. Steve Jobs and Bill Gates were college dropouts, but the market deemed them good. Now that I think of it, apparently Einstein was a mediocre student, but his contributions to science were his way out. With recent advances in AI mathematics, both of these paths to glory are under fire. Clara Collier makes similar points in her exceptional essay “ After Work, We’ll Have Each Other .”

If AI takes our ability to contribute, what’s left for our children?

Neil Postman offers a few suggestions for positive purposes for education that I found heartening, not mainly for their content, but for the fact that it’s possible to make up new purposes for education and advocate for them. My favorite suggestions of Postman’s are:

Spaceship Earth – we’re all in this together; let’s take care of each other and our planet

The American Experiment – let’s revive our sense of wonder, curiosity, and responsibility about what America is and can be

The World Makers – as a student of McLuhan, Postman would be remiss if he didn’t invite students to make the tools and narratives that thereafter make us

At the risk of going too meta, I do strongly believe in Postman’s point (in his other education book, Teaching as a Subversive Activity ) that “the medium is the message.” That the way we teach what we teach is often more important than the what . And likewise, I believe in Dr. Alfie Kohn’s notion that we should relate to our educational charges as humans, not objects – “doing with” vs “doing to”. Thus, I believe it may be most honest and effective to invite our children to help us craft the purpose for their education as we figure it out together.

items.title: Meta’s Muse hits 10M U.S. downloads in 40 days, a milestone reached by only 11 other apps
items.summary: Meta's AI companion Muse has surpassed 10 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days, joining an exclusive group of apps that includes Threads. New data also shows Muse is retaining users at higher rates than its AI rivals.
items.content:
Meta’s AI companion, Muse, is now one of only a dozen mobile apps to have reached 10 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. According to new data from market intelligence provider Sensor Tower, Muse has seen 10.9 million downloads since its September debut, 10.2 million of which were in the United States.

Only 11 other apps to date have reached this type of post-launch milestone, said Sensor Tower’s Senior Insights Analyst Kara Lee. The most recent of these was Meta’s Threads, back in July 2023. Other apps that saw this kind of scale were largely mobile games, Lee noted.

Meta’s success is tied to the company’s ability to scale its new apps by marketing them across its other services, which it has done with both Threads and Muse. Threads was built on top of Instagram’s social graph, and its content has been integrated into both Facebook and Instagram. However, Muse isn’t only benefiting from Meta’s ability to market the AI agent across its family of apps, which today includes 3.6 billion daily active users; the company is also heavily investing in advertising to drive new users to Muse.

Per Sensor Tower’s data, Meta has allocated 39% of its total advertising spend to market Muse in October, up from 23% last month. In addition, Muse now ranks as the 21st largest brand in the U.S. by advertising impressions this month, up from 73rd in September.

Still, marketing an app and retaining users after the initial shine wears off are two different things. In this case, Muse is seeing better retention rates than its AI competitors like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok.

In the U.S., the app had a 30% retention rate after 7 days and a 23% retention rate after 14 days. By comparison, its rivals saw an average of a 19% 7-day retention rate and a 16% 14-day retention rate, according to the firm’s data.

Muse also hit another milestone that demonstrates active engagement with the AI app. Its daily active users reached 2.5 million for the first time on October 16, a 15% week-over-week increase.

Meta’s latest AI app, which can handle various tasks on users’ behalf, has seen breakout success since its debut. It shot up to No. 1 on the App Store, and, at one point, even outpaced some of the metrics ChatGPT saw following its launch. Its latest milestone sees it topping its rivals again, as ChatGPT saw 3.7 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. Grok and Claude saw only 500,000 and 200,000 U.S. downloads, respectively, in their first 40 days.

Globally, ChatGPT beat out Muse, having scaled to around 15 million global downloads in its first 40 days. But this isn’t a fair comparison, as ChatGPT benefited from a wider reach. Muse is only available in the U.S. and Canada for now, while ChatGPT’s app attracted attention from markets like Japan, Brazil, and Germany, too. (Japan, for instance, accounted for 25% of its global installs during its first 40 days.)

Since launching, Muse has retained its No. 1 rank on the U.S. App Store for all days except October 19, when streaming app Kick briefly beat it out. It has since reclaimed the top spot as of Tuesday. Muse has also been No. 1 on Google Play over the past 30 days.

How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity
items.summary: Three Java Champions share how they use GitHub Copilot to solve problems, accelerate development, and keep humans responsible for the results. The post How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
items.content:
AI coding tools can generate code quickly, but speed alone does not solve the hardest software engineering problems. Developers still need to provide context, validate results, protect maintainability, and remain accountable for what ships.

To learn how experienced developers strike that balance, we spoke with three Java Champions, all with over a decade of experience in using Java. They shared concrete examples of using GitHub Copilot in production and open source, along with the practices they use to turn AI-generated output into reliable software.

Here are the tips they shared with us.

GitHub profile: @vladmihalcea

How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently?

I’ve been using it to analyze, design, and implement various features in both Hypersistence Utils and Hypersistence Optimizer.

For example, I’ve been wanting for a long time to develop a web application that provides Optimizer event history so we can see how performance improvement efforts are materializing in application performance. Before AI, I kept postponing this task because it would have taken me weeks to develop. But using Copilot is like having a new team member, so I used it to create an app that will ship in the next version of Hypersistence Optimizer. Instead of weeks, this task took just two days to implement.

What’s your typical usage? Are you using GitHub Copilot as an IDE plugin or the GitHub Copilot app?

I use GitHub Copilot in IntelliJ IDEA because it’s convenient to run while reviewing source code or during a debug session.

It’s very useful as a code assistant, and it helps me speed up both investigations and building prototypes for features that need validation.

I still review the plans and the code that is generated by AI since their goal is to improve my productivity, not replace me entirely. While AI provides the right answer in many situations, there are still times when the response is not satisfactory and requires my intervention.

Can you share some tips and best practices? For example, which skills are you using?

I created my own skills so that whatever text Copilot generates looks like something I wrote by hand.

This skill captures my voice from 65 of my published articles, so a draft comes back sounding like my blog instead of like a language model. This is really useful when generating documentation for this project, since it lets the LLM learn from 12 years of blogging and provide examples that follow the same principles, such as expressiveness, testability, and simplicity.

Throughout my career as a software engineer, I’ve learned that we spend far more time on code maintenance than on creating it. Therefore, because maintenance and stability are critical for existing products, I developed skills that help AI mimic existing code practices in accordance with the principle of least astonishment.

One tip is to change the model type based on the type of operation. For thorough thinking, I use Opus with the 1 million context window and Extra High or Max reasoning. However, for simpler tasks, such as generating reports, release notes, or verifying documentation, I use lighter models that consume fewer tokens.

GitHub profile: @patbaumgartner

Your work involves coaching teams. What is your approach?

A lot of my work happens while the normal business still has to keep running. You cannot stop everything for six months to “transform.” We usually start by solving immediate problems together, understand where the team currently stands, define where we want to go and how we will know that we are improving, and then move there step by step.

Depending on the situation, that can mean Software Craft practices such as TDD, refactoring, continuous delivery and XP; architecture and modularisation with Spring Boot, Spring Modulith; Spring Security; optimising Java and Spring Boot applications for containers; or increasingly, agentic engineering.

The important part for me is that I work with the team. We make decisions together. I don’t want a team to become dependent on me. Ideally, after some time they no longer need me except perhaps as a sparring partner.

And maybe that explains why I find this new generation of AI tools so interesting: I like working with people, learning, experimenting, and solving problems. AI gives us another very powerful tool for doing exactly that.

Can you share a good story about how GitHub Copilot has helped you recently?

There are actually three very different examples that changed how I think about working with GitHub Copilot.

Let’s start with the first one.

One was a migration of around 900 teaching slides across 15 presentations from Reveal.js to Marp. These were not simple slides. Many contain code, animations, and even interactive examples where I can change JavaScript live while teaching. More importantly, the presentations had already been battle-tested with students. The flow worked. Losing one small piece could break the story I use in the classroom.

Doing that migration manually would probably have taken me a week or more—and realistically, I might simply have avoided doing it because it was such tedious work.

With Copilot, I approached it differently. We first analysed the existing material, defined the target, created a migration plan, established constraints, provided examples, and defined what had to remain intact. Then we worked from the big structural changes down into the details.

The really important part was verification.

We generated screenshots of the Reveal.js and Marp versions and compared them visually and algorithmically. We built a small application where I could run both slide decks next to each other to verify animations manually. We even compared the generated PDFs.

That meant the agent did not just say, “Migration complete.” We had evidence.

Speech transcription and voice generation have come a long way, but building end-to-end voice agents that can listen, reason, interact, and handle complex workflows remains difficult.

Listen accurately across languages, accents, speakers, and interruptions,

Reason deeply about what users mean in specific contexts,

Speak naturally with emotion and expression, and

Take action over multiple steps through connected systems.

글로벌뉴스 입력 :2026/10/21 00:10

CAS Connections ℠, 전문가가 직접 선별한 신뢰할 수 있는 과학 지식을 Microsoft Copilot에 통합

콜럼버스, 오하이오 , 2026년 10월 20일 /PRNewswire/ -- 미국화학회(American Chemical Society) 산하 사업부인 CAS가 오늘 Microsoft Copilot에서 CAS Connections를 이용할 수 있게 됐다고 발표했다. 이 커넥터를 통해 Copilot 고객은 CAS Content Collection™과 과학 연구를 위해 개발된 에이전틱 AI인 CAS Newton℠에 접근할 수 있다. CAS와 마이크로소프트(Microsoft)는 제약, 생명과학, 화학 분야 조직의 요구를 고려해 이 커넥터를 개발했다.

이러한 산업의 연구개발(R&D)팀에는 연구자의 고유한 요구에 맞춘 과학 정보와 기능이 필요하다. CAS Connections는 CAS가 150년 이상 선별 및 축적해 온 과학 지식과 CAS Newton의 대화형 지능을 이러한 R&D팀 다수가 매일 문서를 작성하고 분석하며 협업하는 공간인 Copilot에 통합한다. 연구자는 일상적인 업무 흐름에 통합된 엄선된 과학 정보를 활용해 더욱 효율적으로 일하고, 충분한 정보를 바탕으로 의사결정을 내릴 수 있다.

CAS의 팀 월버그(Tim Wahlberg) 사장 직무대행은 "신약 개발과 화학 연구개발에 종사하는 과학자들은 물질, 반응 또는 표적에 관해 알려진 정보를 확인하는 권위 있는 출처로 CAS를 신뢰한다. 마이크로소프트와 협력해 이러한 지식과 고유한 기능들을 Microsoft Copilot에 통합함으로써 연구자들이 초기 구상을 새로운 의약품과 소재로 더욱 빠르게 발전시킬 수 있도록 지원하고 있다"고 말했다.

이 커넥터는 일반적인 연구개발 업무 흐름과의 긴밀한 통합을 지원한다. 예를 들어 Microsoft Word에서 보고서의 실험 부분을 작성하는 화학자는 화합물의 CAS Registry Number® 와 구조를 확인하고, 반응 조건과 시약의 조달 가능 여부를 CAS 기록과 대조하며, 작성 중인 문서에 출처를 인용할 수 있다. Microsoft Teams를 사용하는 지식재산 분석가는 특정 물질이 특허 문헌에 등장하는지 확인할 수 있다. Microsoft PowerPoint에서 라이선싱 브리핑 자료를 준비하는 사업개발 분석가는 CAS 콘텐츠에서 출처를 확인할 수 있는 특허 동향 정보를 추가할 수 있다.

마이크로소프트의 샨트렐 닐슨(Chantrelle Nielsen) Copilot 플랫폼 수석 제품 관리자는 "제약, 생명과학, 화학 분야 고객에게는 신뢰할 수 있는 과학 정보에 기반한 믿을 수 있는 AI가 필요하다. CAS는 이러한 고객에게 필수적인 정보원이기 때문에 CAS를 Microsoft Copilot 커넥터 생태계에 도입하는 것을 전략적 우선 과제로 삼았다. 이제 과학자, 특허 담당팀, 비즈니스 분석가는 Copilot에서 직접 이 신뢰할 수 있는 정보에 손쉽게 접근할 수 있다"고 말했다.

CAS Connections는 마이크로소프트 외에도 R&D팀이 일상적으로 사용하는 다양한 도구에 CAS 콘텐츠와 CAS Newton을 통합할 수 있도록 지원한다. 여기에는 전자 연구 노트(ELN), 실험실 정보 관리 시스템(LIMS), 디스커버리 플랫폼, 기업용 AI 등이 포함된다. CAS 는 2026년 6월 여러 초기 협력 기관과 함께 CAS Connections를 출시했다.

CAS-Microsoft Copilot 커넥터는 Microsoft Marketplace의 다음 주소에서 이용할 수 있다: marketplace.microsoft.com/en-us/product/WA200012172 .

CAS는 전 세계 과학 지식을 연결해 삶의 질을 높이는 획기적인 발견을 가속한다. 과학 데이터 인텔리전스 파트너로서 전 세계 혁신 주체들이 AI의 잠재력을 실현하고 실질적인 성과를 거둘 수 있도록 지원한다. CAS는 과학자가 직접 선별한 데이터로 구성된 세계 최대 규모의 컬렉션을 구축하고 있다. 이 데이터 기반은 과학에 특화된 인사이트 플랫폼 포트폴리오를 뒷받침하며, 연구개발 업무 흐름과 통합돼 더욱 확신 있는 의사결정과 신뢰할 수 있는 예측을 지원한다. 과학 데이터와 AI 기반 발견을 접목하는 선구자로서 CAS는 생명과학, 화학, 소재 분야 리더들에게 획기적인 혁신을 이끄는 고유한 역량과 전문성을 제공한다. CAS는 미국화학회 산하 사업부다. 자세한 내용은 cas.org 에서 확인할 수 있다.
